text.guided:
Most arrows get **turned** by a matrix.
But some special directions only get **stretched** (or shrunk, or flipped). Those are the **eigenvectors**.
For $\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}$, the x-axis and the y-axis stay where they are.
text.fast: An eigenvector v satisfies A·v = λ·v: same line, new length.

examples.games: Like the axis a sprite is stretched along: it does not tilt.
examples.physics: Like the principal axes of a spinning object.
examples.ai: Like the main directions found by PCA.

scene.caption: The axes only stretch: they are eigen-directions.

check.prompt: For the matrix [[2, 0], [0, 3]], which arrow keeps its direction?

text.guided: With $\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{bmatrix}$, the x-axis still does not turn, but there is **another** one: (1, 1) goes to (3, 3), three times longer, same line.

examples.games: Like a diagonal that stays diagonal after a skewed zoom.
examples.physics: Like a stress direction that only stretches.
examples.ai: Like a stable direction of a linear model.

text.guided:
A rotation turns **every** direction.
So a quarter turn $\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$ has **no** real eigenvector.
text.fast: Rotations (other than 0° and 180°) have no real eigenvectors.

examples.games: Like spinning a camera: nothing stays pointing the same way.
examples.physics: Like a turntable: every radius turns.
examples.ai: Like a rotation of the feature space: no direction is preserved.

scene.caption: A quarter turn: every arrow turns.

check.prompt: Does [[0, −1], [1, 0]] have a direction it does not turn?
